name: ATMEGA2560-16AUR
title: ATmega640/1280/1281/2560/2561 8-bit AVR microcontrollers with 64/128/256 Kbytes in-system programmable Flash
summary: A family of five low-power 8-bit AVR RISC microcontrollers running most of their 135 instructions in one clock, up to 16 MIPS at 16 MHz. All have 4 Kbytes EEPROM, 8 Kbytes SRAM, an external memory interface for up to 64 Kbytes, two 8-bit and four 16-bit timer/counters, a real time counter, SPI, a 2-wire interface, a 10-bit ADC, an analog comparator, a watchdog and JTAG; they differ in Flash (64, 128 or 256 Kbytes) and in package, the 100-pin devices bringing 86 I/O lines, four USARTs and 16 ADC channels. ATMEGA2560-16AUR is the 256 Kbyte ATmega2560 in the 100-lead TQFP, rated 0-16 MHz from 4.5 V to 5.5 V.

operation.text: A low-power CMOS 8-bit AVR whose instructions mostly finish in one clock, giving close to 1 MIPS per MHz. All 32 working registers feed the ALU directly, so one instruction reads two registers and writes the result in a single cycle.

Five devices differ only in memory and pin count. Each has 4 Kbytes EEPROM, 8 Kbytes SRAM, a real time counter, six timer/counters with compare and PWM, a byte-oriented 2-wire interface, an SPI port, a JTAG port for test, debug and programming, a watchdog with its own oscillator and a 10-bit ADC whose input stage can be differential with programmable gain. The 100-pin devices (ATmega640/1280/2560) have 86 I/O lines, four USARTs and 16 ADC channels; the 64-pin ones (ATmega1281/2561) have 54 lines, two USARTs and 8 channels, and lose part of the ADC, Timer/Counter4 and Timer/Counter5.

The Flash can be reprogrammed in the circuit over SPI, by a parallel programmer, or by a boot program running on the core over any interface. Boot code keeps running while it rewrites the application section (read-while-write).
Capacitive buttons, sliders and wheels are supported in software by the QTouch library (QTouch and QMatrix acquisition), which handles debouncing and adjacent-key suppression.
Projected retention failures stay well below 1 ppm for 20 years at 85 °C, or for 100 years at 25 °C.

Harvard architecture with separate program and data buses and a one-stage pipeline: the next instruction is fetched while the current one runs, so an instruction can complete every clock. Most instructions are one 16-bit word; every program address holds a 16- or 32-bit instruction. Jumps and calls reach the whole address space. The Flash has a Boot section and an Application section, each with its own lock bits, and an SPM that writes the Application section must run from the Boot section.

64 I/O addresses hold the control registers of the CPU peripherals; they are reached with IN/OUT or as data addresses 0x20 to 0x5F. The extended I/O space, 0x60 to 0x1FF, is reached only by the load and store instructions.

The ALU does arithmetic, logic and bit operations between registers or between a register and a constant in one cycle, and includes a multiplier for signed, unsigned and fractional numbers. Every ALU operation updates the status register (SREG: I global interrupt enable, T bit copy, H half carry, S sign = N xor V, V two's complement overflow, N negative, Z zero, C carry). SREG is not saved or restored on interrupts; software must do it. Hardware clears I when an interrupt is taken; RETI or SEI sets it, CLI clears it.

The 32 registers occupy data addresses 0x00 to 0x1F. R26:R27, R28:R29 and R30:R31 form the 16-bit X, Y and Z pointers for indirect addressing with displacement, post-increment or pre-decrement; Z also points into Flash for table lookups.

The stack grows downward in data SRAM and must be set above 0x0200 before calls or interrupts; at reset SP holds the last internal SRAM address. PUSH and POP move SP by one. A call, interrupt or return moves it by two on ATmega640/1280/1281 and by three on ATmega2560/2561, whose program counter is three bytes. SP is the register pair SPH:SPL in I/O space.

For ELPM and SPM the Z pointer is extended to 24 bits with RAMPZ as the top byte; LPM ignores RAMPZ. For EICALL and EIJMP the target is EIND:ZH:ZL; ICALL and IJMP ignore EIND. Unused bits read 0 and should be written 0.
The CPU runs from clkCPU taken straight from the selected clock source without internal division. A two-operand ALU operation fetches its registers, executes and writes back within one clock.

Each interrupt has its own enable bit, which works only with the global I bit set, and its own vector at the bottom of program memory; a lower vector address has higher priority, RESET first, then INT0. Programming BLB02 or BLB12 can block interrupts depending on where the program counter is. The vectors move to the start of the Boot section by setting IVSEL in MCUCR, and the reset vector moves there by programming the BOOTRST fuse. Entering an interrupt clears I; software may set it to allow nesting, and RETI sets it. Flag-type interrupts set a flag that is remembered until serviced or cleared by writing a one to it; level-type interrupts fire only while their condition lasts. After a return one more instruction of the main program runs before a pending interrupt is taken. Interrupts are off immediately after CLI, even one arriving with it; after SEI the next instruction runs before any pending interrupt, so SEI followed by SLEEP enters sleep first.

At least five clocks from the interrupt to the vector, during which the program counter is pushed; the vector's jump takes three more. A multi-cycle instruction in progress is finished first. Waking from sleep adds five clocks on top of the start-up time. A return from interrupt takes five clocks, popping the three-byte program counter, adding three to SP and setting I.

64K/128K/256 Kbytes organised as 32K/64K/128K x 16, addressed by a 15/16/17-bit program counter, with at least 10,000 write/erase cycles. Constant tables can sit anywhere in program memory and are read with LPM and ELPM. Programming goes through SPI, JTAG or the boot loader.

The first 8,704 data addresses cover the register file (32), standard I/O (64), extended I/O (416) and 8,192 bytes of internal SRAM. An optional external SRAM fills the rest of the 64K data space from the next address up, leaving 56,832 bytes of it usable with a 64 Kbyte part. Addresses above the internal SRAM go to the external SRAM with the same instructions once SRE in XMCRA is set; during internal accesses the RD and WR strobes (PG1, PG0) stay inactive. The five addressing modes are direct (whole data space), indirect with displacement (63 locations from Y or Z), indirect, and indirect with pre-decrement or post-increment.

Each external byte access costs one clock more than internal SRAM, so every load, store, PUSH or POP to it gains a cycle. With the stack in external SRAM, calls, returns and interrupts take three extra clocks for the three-byte program counter. With one, two or three wait states a byte access takes two, three or four extra clocks, and calls, returns and interrupts take five, seven or nine extra.
An internal SRAM access takes two clkCPU cycles.

4 Kbytes in their own address space, read and written a byte at a time, with at least 100,000 write/erase cycles. A read halts the CPU for four clocks and a write for two. Writes are timed by the calibrated RC oscillator (26,368 cycles, 3.3 ms typical) and need a fixed sequence: set EEMPE, then within four cycles set EEPE, with interrupts kept out. When a boot loader is present the write must also wait for any SPM in progress. SPI, JTAG and parallel programming can also load the EEPROM.

With VCC too low the EEPROM write itself can fail, and the CPU can execute instructions wrongly. Holding RESET low while the supply is too low prevents both; the internal brown-out detector does it, or an external low-VCC reset circuit when the BOD levels do not fit. A write in progress when reset arrives still finishes if the supply holds.

All peripherals sit in I/O space and are reached by the load and store instructions. I/O addresses 0x00 to 0x1F are bit-addressable with SBI, CBI, SBIS and SBIC. IN and OUT use I/O addresses 0x00 to 0x3F; as data addresses these are offset by 0x20. Reserved bits should be written 0 and reserved addresses never written. Flags cleared by writing a one may be handled with SBI and CBI, which on this device touch only the named bit. Three general purpose I/O registers are free for globals and flags.

Reaches external SRAM, Flash and peripherals such as displays and converters in the address space above internal SRAM. Features: four wait-state settings (including none), separate wait states for two sectors of configurable size, a selectable number of high address bits, and optional bus keepers on the data lines. Signals: AD7:0 multiplexed low address and data (Port A), A15:8 high address (Port C, width selectable), ALE (PG2), RD (PG1) and WR (PG0). XMCRA and XMCRB hold the controls.

When enabled, the interface overrides the data-direction settings of its ports and decides on each access whether it is internal or external. An external access drives address, data and strobes; the address on AD7:0 is valid when ALE falls, and ALE stays low during the data transfer. Internal accesses still toggle the address, data and ALE lines but not RD and WR. With the interface disabled, addresses above internal SRAM are not mapped to internal SRAM.

The low-address latch must be chosen with care above 8 MHz at 4 V or 4 MHz at 2.7 V, where an old 74HC latch is too slow; the interface is designed to 74AHC timing. The latch's D-to-Q delay adds to the access time the external part must meet, and its setup time before G falls must not exceed tAVLLC less the board wiring delay. Address hold after G falls is at least 5 ns.

Writing ones to the Port A register turns on pull-ups on AD7:0; clear them before sleep to save power. A bus keeper, switched in XMCRB, holds the last value on AD7:0 while the interface leaves the lines tri-stated.

Four wait-state settings fit slower memories, and the space can be split in two sectors with their own settings for two different devices. The memory's access time must fit within the time from ALE low to data stable in a read. The interface is asynchronous: its waveforms follow the internal clock, the skew to XTAL1 is not guaranteed, and it is not suited to synchronous operation. With no wait states a write or read spans T1 to T3; the settings SRWn1:SRWn0 = 01, 10 and 11 stretch the cycle by one, two and three clocks (the following ALE pulse falls in T5, T6 or T7), and an ALE pulse in the last period appears only if the next instruction accesses RAM.

The first 8,704 locations of an external memory are hidden behind internal memory. With a 32 Kbyte part, A15 is left unconnected and addresses 0x8000 to 0xA1FF reach external locations 0x0000 to 0x21FF, so the part appears as one linear space from 0x2200 to 0xA1FF; addresses above 0xA1FF alias locations already reached lower down.

operation.topic: Using all 64 Kbytes of external memory
operation.text: Only 56 Kbytes are reachable by default. Releasing the top address bits with the XMMn bits and driving them low from Port C under software control masks the high address, so the interface reaches 0x0000 to 0x2FFF; most of the memory is then masked away.

Clocks not needed can be stopped by sleep modes. clkCPU drives the core, register file, status register and stack memory; clkI/O drives most I/O modules (timers, SPI, USART) and the external-interrupt logic, though some external interrupts and TWI address recognition work with it stopped; clkFLASH runs the Flash interface with the CPU clock; clkASY lets the asynchronous Timer/Counter run from an external clock or 32 kHz crystal as a real-time counter in sleep; clkADC is a separate domain so the CPU and I/O clocks can stop during conversions to cut noise.
The CKSEL fuses pick the source: low-power crystal, full-swing crystal, low-frequency crystal, internal 128 kHz RC, calibrated internal RC or external clock.

Parts ship running from the internal RC oscillator at 8.0 MHz with CKDIV8 programmed, so the system clock is 1.0 MHz, with the longest start-up time (CKSEL = 0010, SUT = 10, CKDIV8 = 0). Every programming interface works at this setting.

After every other reset source releases, an internal reset is held for a time-out tTOUT counted on the watchdog oscillator, whose length the SUT and CKSEL fuses select (0, 4.1 ms or 65 ms at 5 V). It does not watch VCC, so it must exceed the supply rise time, or a brown-out detector must be used; dropping the time-out without a BOD is not advised. A ripple counter then waits for a number of oscillator cycles, from 6 for an external clock up to 32K for a low-frequency crystal, before releasing reset. Waking from Power-save or Power-down uses only the oscillator start-up time.

XTAL1 and XTAL2 are the input and output of an inverting amplifier for a quartz crystal or ceramic resonator. This mode has a reduced swing on XTAL2: lowest power, but it cannot drive other clock inputs and is more sensitive to noise. C1 and C2 are equal; 12 to 22 pF is a starting point for crystals, and a resonator takes the values its vendor gives. CKSEL3:1 pick one of three frequency ranges, and CKSEL0 with SUT1:0 the start-up time.

Same pins and capacitors as the low-power oscillator, but with rail-to-rail swing on XTAL2, so it can drive other clock inputs and suits noisy surroundings, at higher current. It works only for VCC of 2.7 to 5.5 V and covers 0.4 to 16 MHz with CKSEL3:1 = 011.

A dedicated oscillator for a 32.768 kHz watch crystal, with internal load capacitance at each pin. A crystal whose load capacitance is higher than the pins give needs external capacitors. SUT and CKSEL0 select the start-up time.

Gives about 8 MHz with no external parts; it drifts with voltage and temperature but can be calibrated closely. The factory value is loaded into OSCCAL at reset; writing OSCCAL from software can calibrate it more accurately. The watchdog oscillator still clocks the watchdog and the reset time-out. Range 7.3 to 8.1 MHz with CKSEL = 0010.
A low-power 128 kHz clock, nominal at 3 V and 25 °C, not designed for accuracy; selected with CKSEL = 0011.

An outside clock drives XTAL1, with CKSEL = 0000 and 0 to 16 MHz. A cycle-to-cycle frequency change above 2% can make the part misbehave, so larger changes need the part held in reset; the system clock prescaler gives safe run-time changes instead.
With the CKOUT fuse programmed the system clock, after the prescaler, appears on CLKO (PE7), also during reset, overriding the pin's normal function. Any clock source can be used.
Timer/Counter2 can run from a 32.768 kHz watch crystal on TOSC1/TOSC2 or from an external clock on TOSC1, which needs EXCLK in ASSR set.

CLKPR divides the system clock to save power when little processing is needed; it works with every source and scales clkI/O, clkADC, clkCPU and clkFLASH. Switching produces no glitch and no intermediate frequency above the old or new one. The prescaler's ripple counter runs at the undivided clock, so its state and the exact switching time cannot be known. To change it, write CLKPCE = 1 with the other bits 0, then within four cycles write CLKPS with CLKPCE = 0, with interrupts disabled.

Six sleep modes stop unused clock domains. SE in SMCR must be set and SM2:0 select the mode before a SLEEP instruction. An enabled interrupt wakes the MCU, which halts four cycles beyond the start-up time, runs the interrupt and continues after the SLEEP; register file and SRAM keep their contents. A reset during sleep wakes the part into the reset vector.

SM2:0 = 000. Stops clkCPU and clkFLASH; SPI, USART, analog comparator, ADC, 2-wire interface, timers, watchdog and interrupts keep running, so external and internal interrupts such as timer overflow or USART transmit complete wake it. Setting ACD in ACSR turns the comparator off when its wake-up is not needed. An enabled ADC starts a conversion on entry.

SM2:0 = 001. Stops clkI/O, clkCPU and clkFLASH; the ADC, external interrupts, TWI address match, Timer/Counter2 and watchdog may run, giving the ADC a quieter environment. An enabled ADC starts a conversion on entry. Wake-up sources: ADC conversion complete, external reset, watchdog reset or interrupt, brown-out reset, 2-wire interface, Timer/Counter2, SPM/EEPROM ready, INT7:4 held at a low level, or any pin change.

SM2:0 = 010. The external oscillator stops; external interrupts, the 2-wire interface and the watchdog may run. Wake-up sources: external reset, watchdog reset, brown-out reset, TWI address match, INT7:4 at a low level, INT3:0, or any pin change. A level used for wake-up must be held long enough. Wake-up takes the reset time-out set by the CKSEL fuses.

SM2:0 = 011. As Power-down, but an enabled Timer/Counter2 keeps running and its overflow or compare interrupt can wake the part (with its TIMSK2 enable and the I bit set). Timer/Counter2 can run synchronously or asynchronously; the clock it does not use is stopped, and a running synchronous clock serves only Timer/Counter2. Without Timer/Counter2 running, Power-down is the better choice.
SM2:0 = 110 with an external crystal or resonator selected. As Power-down but the oscillator keeps running; wake-up takes six clock cycles.
SM2:0 = 111 with an external crystal or resonator selected. As Power-save but the oscillator keeps running; wake-up takes six clock cycles.

PRR0 and PRR1 stop the clock of individual peripherals in Active and Idle mode. A stopped peripheral freezes, its registers cannot be read or written, and the pins it holds stay taken; it should usually be disabled first. Clearing the bit brings it back in its earlier state.

Use the deepest sleep mode that works and turn off what is not needed. The ADC stays on in every sleep mode if enabled, and its next conversion after turning back on is an extended one. Disable the analog comparator in Idle and ADC Noise Reduction; in other modes it switches off itself unless it uses the internal reference. An enabled BOD and an enabled watchdog run in every sleep mode and add notably to deep-sleep current. The internal reference runs when the BOD, comparator or ADC needs it, and needs its start-up time after being off. Pins should not drive resistive loads. Where clkI/O and clkADC are both stopped the input buffers are disabled, except those needed for wake-up; a floating input or one near VCC/2 draws excess current, and analog inputs should have their digital buffers disabled in DIDR0, DIDR1 and DIDR2. An on-chip debug system enabled by OCDEN keeps the main clock running in sleep; it is turned off by unprogramming OCDEN or JTAGEN, or writing JTD in MCUCR.

During reset all I/O registers take their initial values and execution starts at the reset vector, which must hold a JMP to the reset handler. Unused interrupt vectors may hold ordinary code. Ports go to their reset state as soon as a reset source is active, with no clock needed. When all sources have released, a delay counter set by SUT and CKSEL stretches the internal reset so the supply can settle.

Five sources: power-on reset (VCC below VPOT), external reset (RESET low longer than the minimum pulse), watchdog reset (watchdog period expires with the watchdog enabled), brown-out reset (AVCC below VBOT with the BOD on) and JTAG AVR reset (a one in the JTAG Reset Register). MCUSR flags which one occurred (PORF, EXTRF, BORF, WDRF, JTRF).

An on-chip detector holds the part in reset while VCC is below its level; reaching the threshold starts the delay counter, and reset reasserts at once when VCC falls below it. It serves both for start-up and for detecting supply failure. RESET may be tied to VCC or held low externally to extend the reset.
A low on RESET longer than the minimum pulse width resets the part even without a clock; shorter pulses may not. When RESET rises through VRST the delay counter starts and the MCU runs after tTOUT.

Compares AVCC with a level set by the BODLEVEL fuses, with hysteresis. Reset asserts at once when AVCC falls below VBOT- and releases tTOUT after AVCC rises above VBOT+. A dip must last longer than tBOD to be seen.
A watchdog time-out gives a reset pulse one CK long; the time-out period tTOUT starts on its falling edge.

A bandgap reference serves the BOD and can feed the analog comparator or the ADC. It runs only when the BOD is enabled by the BODLEVEL fuses, when ACBG in ACSR connects it to the comparator, or when the ADC is enabled. Without the BOD, software must allow its start-up time after setting ACBG or enabling the ADC before using their outputs. Avoiding all three before Power-down turns it off.

Counts cycles of a separate 128 kHz oscillator, with time-outs from 16 ms to 8 s. Three modes: interrupt (for wake-up or as a general timer limiting how long an operation may take), system reset (against runaway code), and interrupt then reset (allows saving state before the reset). The WDR instruction restarts the count. The WDTON fuse forces system reset mode, locking WDE to 1 and WDIE to 0.

To clear WDE or change the time-out: write WDCE and WDE to one together (WDE one whatever it held), then within four clocks write WDE and WDP as wanted with WDCE cleared, in one operation, with interrupts kept out. Reset the watchdog before changing WDP, since a shorter period can time out at once. A watchdog enabled by accident stays enabled after the reset it causes, so start-up code should clear WDRF and WDE even when the watchdog is unused, or the part can keep resetting.

Every port supports read-modify-write: SBI and CBI change one pin's direction, output value or pull-up without touching others. Outputs sink and source symmetrically and can drive LED displays directly. Each pin has a selectable pull-up whose resistance does not change with supply, and protection diodes to VCC and ground. Each port has three registers: PORTx (data), DDRx (direction) and PINx (input, read-only). Writing a one to a PINx bit toggles the PORTx bit, whatever DDRx holds. PUD in MCUCR turns off every pull-up. Enabling an alternate function on some pins leaves the others usable as I/O.

DDxn = 1 makes the pin an output, driving PORTxn; DDxn = 0 makes it an input, with the pull-up on when PORTxn = 1. Pins go high-impedance during reset with no clock needed. Going between tri-state (00) and output high (11) passes through pull-up (01) or output low (10); PUD can disable pull-ups if the pull-up state is a problem. Going from pulled-up input to driven-low output (or back) likewise needs tri-state or output high as the step between.

PINxn reads the pin whatever the direction, through a latch and flip-flop synchronizer that delays a change by between half and one and a half system clocks. To read back a value just written, put a NOP between the OUT and the IN; the delay through the synchronizer is then one clock.

In Power-down, Power-save and Standby the sleep controller clamps the Schmitt-trigger input to ground so floating or mid-level inputs draw no current. Pins enabled as external interrupts, and some alternate functions, override the clamp. A high level on an asynchronous external interrupt pin set for rising, falling or any edge, with the interrupt disabled, sets its flag on waking, because the clamp release looks like an edge.

Give unused pins a defined level to save current in Active, Idle and reset, where inputs are enabled. The internal pull-up is simplest, but it is off during reset; an external resistor to either rail covers reset too. Tying a pin straight to VCC or GND risks a large current if it is ever set as an output.

Alternate functions take over a pin through override signals generated by the module: pull-up (PUOE, PUOV), direction (DDOE, DDOV), output value (PVOE, PVOV), toggle (PTOE) and digital input enable (DIEOE, DIEOV); DI feeds the module and AIO connects analog signals straight to the pad.

OC0A, OC1A, OC1B, OC1C and OC2A outputs need the pin set as output. With SPI as master, MISO is forced to input; as slave, MOSI, SCK and SS are forced to input, and the slave SPI is active while SS is low. A pin forced to input keeps its pull-up under PORTB control. On the 100-pin devices the serial-programming data lines are on MOSI and MISO.

XCK1 is an output when DDD5 is set and works only in synchronous USART mode. TXD1 is forced to output when the transmitter is on, RXD1 to input when the receiver is on, with the pull-up still under PORTD2. With TWEN set, PD0 and PD1 leave the port and become SCL and SDA, with a 50 ns spike filter on the input and an open-drain, slew-rate-limited driver.

CLKO on PE7 outputs the divided system clock whenever CKOUT is programmed, ignoring PORTE7 and DDE7, and also during reset. AIN0 and AIN1 connect directly to the analog comparator inputs. XCK0 is an output when DDE2 is set and works only in synchronous mode. RXD0 is forced to input with the receiver on, and PORTE0 still switches its pull-up. On the 64-pin devices PE0 and PE1 also carry the serial-programming data input and output.

Port F holds ADC inputs 0 to 7. Port F pins set as outputs must not switch during a conversion or they can corrupt it. With JTAG enabled, PF4 to PF7 serve as TCK, TMS, TDO and TDI and cannot be used as I/O, the pull-ups on TCK, TMS and TDI stay on through reset, and TDO is tri-stated except in the shift states.
With AS2 in ASSR set, PG4 and PG3 leave the port and become the input and output of the Timer/Counter2 crystal amplifier. PG2, PG1 and PG0 are ALE, RD and WR of the external memory interface.

operation.topic: Ports H to L alternate functions
operation.text: Port H carries USART2 and the Timer/Counter4 outputs, Port J USART3 and pin-change inputs 9 to 15, Port K ADC inputs 8 to 15 and pin-change inputs 16 to 23, and Port L the Timer/Counter5 outputs and the input captures of Timer/Counters 4 and 5. XCK2 and XCK3 are outputs when their DDR bit is set and work only in synchronous mode; RXD2 and RXD3 are forced to input with the receiver on, with the pull-up under the PORT bit.

57 vectors two words apart from 0x0000; vectors 12 (PCINT2), 42 (TIMER4 CAPT), 47 (TIMER5 CAPT) and 52 to 57 (USART2 and USART3) exist only on ATmega640/1280/2560. A program that enables no interrupts may put ordinary code in the vector area; the same holds when reset and interrupt vectors are in different sections. The usual layout puts a JMP to each handler at its vector, then the main program sets the stack pointer to RAMEND and enables interrupts.

MCUCR places the vector table. Changing IVSEL needs a timed sequence: write IVCE to one, then write the wanted IVSEL value (with IVCE zero) in the next operation. With an 8 Kbyte boot section the boot reset address is 0x1F000 and the moved interrupt vectors start at 0x1F002.

INT7:0 and PCINT23:0 trigger interrupts, also when the pins are outputs, which gives a way to make software interrupts. PCI2 fires on any enabled change of PCINT23:16, PCI1 of PCINT15:8 and PCI0 of PCINT7:0, with PCMSK2, PCMSK1 and PCMSK0 choosing the pins; pin-change interrupts are detected asynchronously, so they also wake the part from sleep modes other than Idle. INT7:0 trigger on either edge or on a low level, set in EICRA (INT3:0) and EICRB (INT7:4); a level interrupt keeps firing while the pin is low. Low levels and the INT3:0 edges are detected asynchronously and wake the part from modes other than Idle. A level used to wake from Power-down must last until the start-up time ends, or the part wakes with no interrupt.
A pin change passes through a latch and synchronizer clocked by the system clock before setting PCIF, taking a few clock cycles from the pin edge to the flag.

An 8-bit timer/counter with two output compare units (A and B), double-buffered compare registers, clear on compare match, glitch-free phase correct PWM, a variable PWM period and a frequency generator. It raises three interrupts: overflow TOV0 and the compare matches OCF0A and OCF0B, flagged in TIFR0 and masked in TIMSK0.

The counter runs from the shared prescaler or from an external clock on the T0 pin, chosen by CS02:0 in TCCR0B; with no source chosen (CS02:0 = 0) it stops, though TCNT0 can still be read and written. A CPU write to TCNT0 wins over any count or clear in the same cycle.

The comparator matches TCNT0 against OCR0A and OCR0B continuously; a match sets OCF0A or OCF0B on the next timer clock, which can interrupt and is cleared by the interrupt or by writing one to it. OCR0x is double buffered in the PWM modes, updating at TOP or BOTTOM so pulses stay whole, and written directly in Normal and CTC modes. Writing FOC0x in a non-PWM mode forces the pin action of a match without setting the flag or clearing the timer. Any CPU write to TCNT0 blocks a compare match in the following timer clock, even with the timer stopped, so writing TCNT0 equal to OCR0x loses that match.

When either COM0x1:0 bit is set, the waveform generator takes over the OC0x pin from the port, but the pin only drives once its DDR bit makes it an output; set the OC0x state (FOC0x in Normal mode is the simplest way) before enabling the output. A reset clears the internal OC0x register to 0. COM0x1:0 changes take effect at once and are not double buffered; with COM0x1:0 = 0 a match leaves OC0x alone.

WGM02:0 = 0. The counter only counts up, wrapping from 0xFF to 0x00; TOV0 sets in the clock where TCNT0 becomes zero and acts as a ninth bit that software must clear (the overflow interrupt clears it). TCNT0 can be written at any time.

WGM02:0 = 2. TCNT0 clears to zero when it matches OCR0A, so OCR0A sets the top and the resolution; OCF0A can interrupt at each top. CTC has no double buffering of OCR0A: writing a value below the current count misses the match and the counter runs on to 0xFF and wraps first. With COM0A1:0 = 1 the OC0A pin toggles on each match, up to fclk_I/O/2 with OCR0A = 0. TOV0 sets when the count passes MAX to 0x00.

WGM02:0 = 3 (TOP = 0xFF) or 7 (TOP = OCR0A). A single-slope count from BOTTOM to TOP, so up to twice the frequency of phase correct PWM. Non-inverting (COM0x1:0 = 2): OC0x clears on the match and sets at BOTTOM; inverting (3) does the reverse. COM0A1:0 = 1 with WGM02 set toggles OC0A on matches (not available on OC0B), giving a 50% wave up to fclk_I/O/2. TOV0 sets at TOP. OCR0A = BOTTOM gives a narrow spike every MAX+1 clocks; OCR0A = MAX gives a constant level.

WGM02:0 = 1 (TOP = 0xFF) or 5 (TOP = OCR0A). A dual-slope count up to TOP and back to BOTTOM, staying one clock at TOP; symmetric, and favoured for motor control. Non-inverting: OC0x clears on the up-count match and sets on the down-count match. TOV0 sets at BOTTOM. OCR0A = BOTTOM holds the non-inverted output low and MAX holds it high. The output can also change at BOTTOM with no match, to keep symmetry, when OCR0A moves away from MAX or the counter starts above OCR0A.

The timer is synchronous: clkT0 acts as a clock enable on clk_I/O. TOV0 and OCF0x set one timer clock after the count reaches MAX or OCR0x; in CTC and in fast PWM with OCR0A as TOP the counter clears to BOTTOM and OCF0A sets in the clock after TOP.

Four 16-bit timer/counters, each with three output compare units (A, B, C), double-buffered compare registers, one input capture unit with a noise canceler, clear on compare match, glitch-free phase correct PWM, a variable PWM period, a frequency generator and an external event counter; 20 interrupt sources in all (TOVn, OCFnA, OCFnB, OCFnC and ICFn for each). PRTIM1 in PRR0 and PRTIM3, PRTIM4 and PRTIM5 in PRR1 must be zero for the timer to run. Timer/Counter4 and 5 are complete only on the ATmega640/1280/2560: the ATmega1281/2561 have no input capture or output compare on them.

TCNTn, OCRnA/B/C and ICRn are 16 bits wide; TCCRnA/B/C are 8-bit control registers with no access limits. Flags sit in TIFRn and masks in TIMSKn. TOP can be a fixed value, OCRnA or ICRn; when OCRnA is TOP in a PWM mode it cannot also drive a PWM output, but TOP is then double buffered, while ICRn as TOP leaves OCRnA free.

The CPU reaches the 16-bit registers in two byte accesses through one 8-bit temporary register (TEMP) per timer, shared by all of that timer's 16-bit registers. Write the high byte first, then the low byte, which moves both into place in one clock; read the low byte first, which copies the high byte into TEMP for the next read. Reading OCRnA/B/C does not use TEMP. In C the compiler orders the bytes. An interrupt that touches any 16-bit register of the same timer between the two accesses corrupts TEMP, so code that shares them with interrupts disables interrupts around each access. When several registers get the same high byte, it need be written only once.

CSn2:0 in TCCRnB picks the prescaler tap or the Tn pin; CSn2:0 = 0 stops the counter, which stays readable and writable. TCNTnH is reached only through TEMP. The count sequence is set by WGMn3:0 across TCCRnA and TCCRnB, and writing TCNTn while it counts can give unpredictable results in some cases.

An edge on the ICPn pin, or for Timer/Counter1 only on the analog comparator output (selected by ACIC in ACSR), copies TCNTn into ICRn and sets ICFn in the same system clock; ICFn interrupts if TICIEn = 1 and clears when the interrupt runs or when one is written to it. Read ICRnL before ICRnH. ICRn can be written only in modes that use it as TOP, after WGMn3:0 is set, high byte first. Changing the trigger source can cause a capture, so clear ICFn afterwards. Inputs are sampled like the Tn pin; the noise canceler (ICNCn in TCCRnB) needs four equal samples to pass a change and adds four system clocks of delay, independent of the prescaler. The capture input is active unless ICRn is TOP. Writing the ICPn port bit triggers a capture from software.

Each new event overwrites ICRn, so read it early in the interrupt; the worst case response depends on the longest other interrupt handler. Changing TOP while capturing is not advised. To measure duty cycle, switch the edge after each capture and then clear ICFn; for frequency alone with an interrupt handler, clearing is not needed. In Normal mode the time between events must fit the counter, or the overflow interrupt or prescaler must extend it.

Each unit compares TCNTn with OCRnx continuously and sets OCFnx on the next timer clock after a match, interrupting if OCIEnx = 1. Unit A can also set TOP and with it the waveform period. OCRnx is double buffered in all twelve PWM modes (updated at TOP or BOTTOM) and direct in Normal and CTC. Writing OCRnx goes through TEMP, high byte first. FOCnx forces a match action in non-PWM modes without setting the flag. A TCNTn write blocks a match in the next timer clock; writing TCNTn equal to TOP in a variable-TOP PWM mode skips TOP and the counter runs to 0xFFFF. Set the OCnx state before making the pin an output; COMnx1:0 changes take effect at once. COMnx1:0 does not affect input capture.
WGMn3:0 = 0. Counts up and wraps from 0xFFFF to 0x0000; TOVn sets as TCNTn becomes zero and works as a 17th bit. TCNTn may be written at any time.

WGMn3:0 = 4 (TOP = OCRnA) or 12 (TOP = ICRn). TCNTn clears on a match with TOP; OCFnA or ICFn flags each top. CTC buffers neither register, so a new TOP below the current count wraps through 0xFFFF first; fast PWM with OCRnA as TOP (mode 15) avoids this. COMnA1:0 = 1 toggles OCnA on each match, at most fclk_I/O/2 with OCRnA = 0. TOVn sets passing MAX to 0x0000.

WGMn3:0 = 5, 6 or 7 (TOP fixed at 0x00FF, 0x01FF or 0x03FF), 14 (TOP = ICRn) or 15 (TOP = OCRnA). Single slope from BOTTOM to TOP; resolution from 2 bits (TOP = 0x0003) to 16 bits (TOP = MAX). TOVn sets at TOP, and OCFnA or ICFn sets with it when that register is TOP. A new TOP must not be below any compare register or that match never happens; with a fixed TOP, unused high bits are masked to zero when an OCRnx register is written. ICRn is not double buffered (a low new value can be missed); OCRnA is, updating as the counter clears, so OCRnA suits a changing period and ICRn a fixed one. COMnx1:0 = 2 gives non-inverted and 3 inverted PWM. OCRnx = BOTTOM gives a one-clock spike every TOP+1 clocks; OCRnx = TOP a steady level. With mode 15 and COMnA1:0 = 1, OCnA toggles at 50% duty, up to fclk_I/O/2.

WGMn3:0 = 1, 2 or 3 (TOP fixed at 0x00FF, 0x01FF or 0x03FF), 10 (TOP = ICRn) or 11 (TOP = OCRnA). Dual slope, 2 to 16 bits of resolution. OCRnx updates at TOP, so changing TOP while running makes the falling slope follow the old TOP and the rising slope the new one, giving an asymmetric period; phase and frequency correct mode is the choice for a changing TOP. TOVn sets at BOTTOM; OCFnA or ICFn sets at TOP when that register is TOP. OCRnx = BOTTOM holds the non-inverted output low and TOP holds it high. Mode 11 with COM1A1:0 = 1 toggles OC1A at 50% duty.

operation.topic: 16-bit Timer/Counter phase and frequency correct PWM mode
operation.text: WGMn3:0 = 8 (TOP = ICRn) or 9 (TOP = OCRnA). Dual slope like phase correct, but OCRnx updates at BOTTOM, so both slopes of every period are equal and the output stays symmetric when TOP changes. Resolution 2 to 16 bits. TOVn sets with the update at BOTTOM; OCFnA or ICFn sets at TOP. Mode 9 with COM1A1:0 = 1 toggles OC1A at 50% duty.

clkTn acts as a clock enable on clk_I/O. OCFnx sets one timer clock after TCNTn equals OCRnx. In CTC and fast PWM the counter goes TOP to BOTTOM; in the dual-slope modes it turns at TOP. TOVn (fast PWM), ICFn when ICRn is TOP, and the OCRnx update at TOP happen in the clock after TOP; in phase and frequency correct mode the same events fall at BOTTOM.

These timers share one free-running prescaler, each with its own setting. CSn2:0 = 1 clocks the timer at fclk_I/O; the prescaler taps give fclk_I/O/8, /64, /256 or /1024. The prescaler does not restart when a timer is enabled, so the first count comes 1 to N+1 system clocks later (N the divisor). Resetting the prescaler (PSR10) synchronizes a timer to program flow but affects every timer that uses it.

The Tn pin is sampled each system clock through a synchronizer and edge detector; CSn2:0 = 7 counts rising edges and 6 falling edges. An edge reaches the counter 2.5 to 3.5 system clocks later. Change the clock selection only while Tn has been steady for a system clock, or a false count can occur. Each half period must exceed one system clock: fExtClk < fclk_I/O/2 at 50% duty, and below fclk_I/O/2.5 is advised to allow for oscillator tolerance. An external clock is not prescaled.

Timer/Counter1 compare unit C (OC1C) and Timer/Counter0 compare unit A (OC0A) share pin PB7. Either one overrides PORTB7 when its COMnx1:0 is non-zero; with both enabled the modulator switches on and combines them: PORTB7 = 0 gives a logical AND of the two outputs and PORTB7 = 1 a logical OR. DDRB7 still sets the pin direction.

Modulation lowers the PWM resolution of OC1C by the number of system clocks in one carrier period of OC0A; with OC1C in fast PWM and OC0A toggling in CTC mode at one clock per half period, resolution halves.

An 8-bit timer/counter with two compare outputs (OC2A, OC2B), clear on compare match, glitch-free phase correct PWM, a frequency generator, a 10-bit prescaler and interrupts TOV2, OCF2A and OCF2B (in TIFR2, masked by TIMSK2). It can run from its own 32 kHz watch crystal, apart from the I/O clock. PRTIM2 in PRR0 must be zero.

By default clkT2 is the I/O clock. Writing AS2 in ASSR to one clocks it from the timer oscillator on TOSC1 and TOSC2. CS22:0 = 0 stops the counter. The count sequence is set by WGM21:0 in TCCR2A and WGM22 in TCCR2B.

Normal (WGM22:0 = 0), CTC (2, TOP = OCR2A), fast PWM (3 with TOP = 0xFF, 7 with TOP = OCR2A) and phase correct PWM (1 with TOP = 0xFF, 5 with TOP = OCR2A) behave as on Timer/Counter0, with OC2A and OC2B in place of OC0A and OC0B; the prescale factor N can also be 32 or 128. CTC toggling reaches fclk_I/O/2 with OCR2A = 0.

Matches between TCNT2 and OCR2A or OCR2B set OCF2A or OCF2B on the next timer clock. OCR2x is double buffered in PWM modes and direct in Normal and CTC. FOC2x forces a match action in non-PWM modes; a TCNT2 write blocks a match in the next timer clock. The OC2x pin drives only when COM2x1:0 is non-zero and its DDR bit is set. In asynchronous mode the timing figures hold with the timer oscillator clock in place of clk_I/O.

Switching between synchronous and asynchronous clocking can corrupt TCNT2, OCR2x and TCCR2x. A safe switch: disable the Timer/Counter2 interrupts (OCIE2x, TOIE2); set AS2; write TCNT2, OCR2x and TCCR2x; when going asynchronous wait for TCN2UB, OCR2xUB and TCR2xUB to clear; clear the Timer/Counter2 flags; re-enable interrupts. The CPU clock must exceed four times the timer oscillator frequency. Writes to TCNT2, OCR2x and TCCR2x pass through a temporary register per register and land after two rising edges on TOSC1; the update busy bits in ASSR show when each has landed, and a new value must not be written before then.

Before entering Power-save or ADC Noise Reduction with Timer/Counter2 as the wake source, wait until any written register has updated; compare matches are disabled while OCR2x or TCNT2 is being written, so sleeping early can leave the part never waking. The interrupt logic needs one TOSC1 cycle to reset after a wake: if the part sleeps again sooner, it will not wake. To be sure a cycle has passed, write TCCR2x, TCNT2 or OCR2x, wait for its busy flag to clear, then sleep.

In asynchronous mode the 32.768 kHz oscillator runs in every mode except Power-down and Standby. After a power-up reset or a wake from Power-down or Standby it may need up to one second to settle; wait that long before using the timer, and treat all Timer/Counter2 registers as lost after a wake from Power-down or Standby, whether a crystal or an external clock on TOSC1 is used.

On an asynchronous interrupt the wake starts on the next timer clock, so the count is always at least one higher by the time the CPU can read it; the CPU then halts four cycles, runs the interrupt and resumes after SLEEP. Just after a wake from Power-save, TCNT2 reads its pre-sleep value until the next rising TOSC1 edge; to read it reliably, write OCR2x or TCCR2x, wait for that busy flag to clear, then read TCNT2. Interrupt flags take three processor cycles plus one timer cycle to synchronize. The OC2x pins change on the timer clock, not synchronized to the CPU clock.

The source clkT2S is clk_I/O by default, or with AS2 set the TOSC1 pin, which makes Timer/Counter2 usable as a real time counter: TOSC1 and TOSC2 leave Port C (the pins of the timer oscillator) and take a crystal, the oscillator being tuned for 32.768 kHz. Setting EXCLK in ASSR accepts a 32 kHz external clock instead. Selections are clkT2S, /8, /32, /64, /128, /256, /1024 and stop. PSRASY in GTCCR resets the prescaler.

A full-duplex three-wire synchronous serial port, master or slave, LSB or MSB first, with seven bit rates, an end-of-transmission interrupt flag, write collision protection, wake-up from Idle and a double speed (CK/2) master mode. The clock divider gives /2, /4, /8, /16, /32, /64 or /128. The USARTs also offer a master SPI mode. PRSPI in PRR0 must be zero.

The master starts a transfer by pulling the slave's S̅S̅ low; both load their shift registers, and the master's SCK clocks data out on MOSI and in on MISO. As master the SPI does not drive S̅S̅ itself: software does. Writing SPDR starts the clock; after eight bits it stops and sets SPIF, interrupting if SPIE is set. As slave, MISO stays tri-stated while S̅S̅ is high and data written to SPDR waits until S̅S̅ goes low. Transmit is single buffered (SPDR cannot be written until the shift is done); receive is double buffered, the received byte having to be read before the next one completes. In slave mode SCK low and high periods must each be longer than two CPU clocks.

In slave mode S̅S̅ is always an input: low activates the SPI and lets MISO drive if set as output; high makes every pin an input, resets the SPI logic and drops a partly received byte, which keeps packets in step. In master mode, S̅S̅ set as output is an ordinary output. Set as input, it must be held high: if it is pulled low the SPI takes it as another master selecting it, clears MSTR (MOSI and SCK become inputs) and sets SPIF. An interrupt-driven master that might see this should check MSTR in its handler and set it again.
Data is shifted out and latched in on opposite SCK edges. DORD = 0 sends MSB first, DORD = 1 LSB first.

Four USARTs (USART0 to USART3) on the ATmega640/1280/2560, each with its own registers: full duplex, asynchronous or synchronous, master or slave synchronous clocking, a high resolution baud rate generator, frames of 5 to 9 data bits with 1 or 2 stop bits, hardware odd or even parity, overrun and framing error detection, false start bit detection with a digital low pass filter, separate interrupts when a frame is fully sent, when the transmit buffer empties and when a frame arrives, a multi-processor mode and a double speed asynchronous mode. PRUSART0 in PRR0 and PRUSART1 to PRUSART3 in PRR1 must be zero to use each one.

Three parts: the clock generator (baud rate generator and a synchronizer for an external clock on XCKn, which is used only in synchronous mode); the transmitter (one write buffer, a shift register, parity generator and control, allowing back-to-back frames); and the receiver (clock and data recovery, parity checker, shift register and a receive buffer two characters deep in UDRn), which flags frame errors, data overrun and parity errors.

Four clock modes: asynchronous at normal or double speed, and synchronous as master or as slave. UMSELn in UCSRnC picks asynchronous or synchronous; U2Xn in UCSRnA doubles the asynchronous speed. In synchronous mode the XCKn DDR bit makes the clock internal (master, output) or external (slave, input).

A down-counter running at fosc reloads from UBRRn each time it reaches zero or UBRRnL is written, giving a clock of fosc/(UBRRn+1). The transmitter divides it by 2, 8 or 16 by mode; the receiver's recovery units use it directly with 2, 8 or 16 states per bit. UBRRn holds 0 to 4095.

U2Xn = 1 halves the asynchronous divisor from 16 to 8 and so doubles the rate; the receiver then takes 8 samples per bit instead of 16, needing a more accurate baud rate and system clock. It has no effect on synchronous mode, where it should be zero.

In synchronous mode XCKn is the clock input (slave) or output (master), and RxDn is sampled on the opposite XCKn edge to the one that changes TxDn. UCPOLn = 0 changes data on the rising edge and samples on the falling; UCPOLn = 1 the reverse.

A frame is one start bit (low), 5 to 9 data bits LSB first, an optional even or odd parity bit, and one or two stop bits (high): 30 combinations. The idle line is high. UCSZn2:0 sets the character size, UPMn1:0 parity and USBSn the stop bits, shared by receiver and transmitter; changing them breaks transfers in progress. The receiver checks only the first stop bit, so a frame error is seen only when that bit is zero.

Set the baud rate, the frame format and enable the transmitter and/or receiver; with interrupts in use, clear the global interrupt flag while doing so. Before changing baud rate or frame format, make sure nothing is in flight: TXCn shows the transmitter done (clear it before each UDRn write if used this way) and RXCn shows no unread data.

TXENn in UCSRnB enables it and takes over the TxDn pin (and XCKn as the clock in synchronous mode). Writing UDRn fills the transmit buffer, which moves to the shift register when it is idle, or as soon as the preceding frame's final stop bit has gone out. With fewer than eight data bits, unused high bits of UDRn are ignored. For 9-bit characters (UCSZn = 7) write the ninth bit to TXB8n before the low byte in UDRn; the ninth bit can mark an address frame in multi-processor mode.

UDREn is set while the transmit buffer is empty and can accept data; with UDRIEn set the data register empty interrupt repeats for as long as UDREn is set, so the handler must write UDRn or disable the interrupt. Write UDREn as zero when writing UCSRnA. TXCn sets when the whole frame has left the shift register and no new data waits; it clears when its interrupt (TXCIEn) runs or by writing one, and suits half-duplex buses such as RS-485 where the transmitter must release the line at once. With parity enabled (UPMn1 = 1) the parity bit is placed after the data bits, ahead of the stop bits. Clearing TXENn takes effect only after pending and ongoing transmissions finish, then frees TxDn.

RXENn enables it and takes over RxDn. Reception begins at a valid start bit; bits are sampled at the baud rate or on XCKn into the shift register until the first stop bit, a second stop bit being ignored, then the frame moves to the receive buffer read through UDRn. With fewer than eight data bits the unused high bits read as zero. For 9-bit characters read RXB8n in UCSRnB before UDRn; the same goes for FEn, DORn and UPEn: read UCSRnA, then UDRn, because reading UDRn advances the receive FIFO that holds these bits.

RXCn is set while unread data is in the receive buffer and clears when the receiver is disabled (which flushes the buffer); with RXCIEn set the interrupt repeats until UDRn is read. The error flags FEn (first stop bit read as zero), DORn (buffer full with two characters, a third in the shift register and a new start bit seen) and UPEn (parity error, with parity checking on) travel in the buffer with their frame, cannot be written by software and raise no interrupt; write them as zero when writing UCSRnA. UPMn1 enables the parity checker and UPMn0 picks odd or even.

Unlike the transmitter, clearing RXENn takes effect at once: a frame in progress is lost, RxDn returns to the port and the buffer FIFO is flushed. To flush during operation, read UDRn until RXCn clears.

The receiver samples at 16 times the baud rate in normal mode and 8 times in double speed mode. A high to low edge on RxDn starts start-bit detection; samples 8, 9 and 10 (normal) or 4, 5 and 6 (double speed) decide by majority: two or three highs reject the edge as noise. A valid start bit resynchronizes the recovery clock, for every frame.

Each bit, parity and the stop bit are decided by majority vote of the three centre samples (16 states per bit in normal mode, 8 in double speed), which also low-pass filters RxDn. A stop bit read as 0 sets FEn. The next start bit may begin right after the last voting sample of the stop bit in normal mode; in double speed mode it must come a little later. This early detection sets the receiver's tolerance range.

The receiver's error comes from its system clock, which drifts a little with supply and temperature (seldom an issue with a crystal; a resonator may be off by more than 2%), and from UBRRn not dividing the clock exactly, where a value giving a low enough error is chosen.

MPCMn in UCSRnA makes the receiver drop frames that carry no address. With 5 to 8 data bits the first stop bit marks the frame type; with 9 data bits RXB8n does. Type bit 1 is an address frame, 0 a data frame. The transmitter is not affected. A master sends 9-bit frames with TXB8n = 1 for an address and 0 for data. All slaves start with MPCMn set and read each address frame; the addressed slave clears MPCMn and takes the data frames, the rest ignore them, and after the last data frame the addressed slave sets MPCMn again to wait for the next address. With 5 to 8 bit frames the transmitter needs two stop bits (USBSn = 1). Do not change MPCMn with SBI or CBI: it shares an I/O location with TXCn, which they can clear by accident.

Tables of UBRR values cover common crystal and resonator frequencies. Settings within 0.5% of the target rate are the preferred ones; larger errors still work but cut the receiver's noise margin, more so for long frames.

Setting both UMSELn1:0 bits to one turns a USART into an SPI master: full duplex three-wire, all four SPI modes, LSB or MSB first, double-buffered (queued) operation, the high resolution baud rate generator, up to fXCKmax = fCK/2 and flexible interrupts. SPI transfer control replaces the USART's RX and TX control; the parity logic and clock and data recovery are off; pins, interrupts and register addresses stay the same.

Master timing and UCPOLn, UCPHAn and UDORDn match the SPI's CPOL, CPHA and DORD. Differences: master only; the transmitter is buffered (the SPI has none) and the receiver has an extra buffer level; there is no WCOL and no SPI2X (UBRRn gives the same effect); interrupt timing and pin control differ.
Only the internal clock is supported, so the XCKn DDR bit must be one (output), preferably before TXENn and RXENn are set. The baud rate follows the synchronous master equation.

A frame is 8 data bits, MSB or LSB first by UDORDn; two writes to UDRn make a 16-bit transfer, signalled done by the transmit complete interrupt. To start: set XCKn as output, set the mode and frame format, enable the transmitter (the receiver is optional; only the transmitter can run alone), then write UBRRn. UBRRn must be zero when the transmitter is enabled so XCKn starts at once, and be written to its working value after enabling but before the first transfer; after a reset it is already zero. Before reconfiguring, check TXCn and RXCn as for the normal USART.

The transmitter must be enabled; writing UDRn starts every transfer, receive included, since the transmitter drives the clock. Read UDRn once for every byte sent to keep the receive buffer in step: on overflow the newest byte is lost, not the oldest. RXCn, TXCn and UDREn work as in normal mode; FE, DOR and PE are unused and read zero. Disabling works as in normal mode.

A two-line bus (SCL clock, SDA data) for master and slave operation, transmit or receive, with 7-bit addresses for up to 128 slaves, multi-master arbitration, transfer rates up to 400 kHz, slew-rate limited outputs, spike suppression on the inputs, a fully programmable slave address with general call, and address recognition that wakes the part from sleep. Each line needs one pull-up resistor. PRTWI in PRR0 must be zero.

Both lines are pulled up to the supply; every device drives them open-drain or open-collector, giving a wired-AND: any device driving low makes the line low. Every AVR on the bus must be powered for the bus to work. The number of devices is limited by the 400 pF bus capacitance and the 7-bit address space; the electrical characteristics come in a set for up to 100 kHz and a set for up to 400 kHz.

SDA must be stable while SCL is high, except for START (SDA falls while SCL is high) and STOP (SDA rises while SCL is high). The bus is busy from a START to a STOP. A START sent while the bus is busy is a REPEATED START, which lets the master begin a new transfer without releasing the bus.

An address packet is 9 bits: 7 address bits MSB first, a READ/WRITE bit (1 = read) and an acknowledge bit, driven low by the addressed slave in the ninth clock; a busy slave leaves SDA high. SLA+R and SLA+W name the packets. Address 0000 000 is the general call, which slaves set up for it acknowledge; it is used with a write bit, a read after general call being meaningless. Addresses 1111 xxx are reserved. A data packet is one byte MSB first plus an acknowledge from the receiver; the receiver signals the last byte with a NACK. A transfer is START, SLA+R/W, at least one data packet, then STOP; START followed directly by STOP is not allowed. A slave can stretch the SCL low period to slow the transfer; the master sets the high period.

The wired-AND combines the SCL of all masters into one clock whose high period is the shortest and low period the longest of the masters'; all masters time their high and low periods from the combined line. Each master watches SDA after driving it: a master that drives high while SDA reads low has lost and must stop driving SDA, may clock to the end of the current packet, and switches to slave mode in case it is addressed. Arbitration may run into the data when masters address the same slave. Arbitration between a REPEATED START and a data bit, a STOP and a data bit, or a REPEATED START and a STOP is not allowed, so all masters' transfers must have the same structure of SLA+R/W and data packets.

operation.topic: TWI pins and bit rate generator
operation.text: The SCL and SDA output drivers have slew-rate limiting; the inputs suppress spikes shorter than 50 ns. The internal pull-ups can be turned on through the PORT bits and may replace external pull-ups in some systems. The bit rate generator sets the SCL period in master mode from TWBR and the prescaler bits TWPS in TWSR. Slave operation does not use them, but the slave's CPU clock must be at least 16 times SCL. Slaves stretching SCL lower the average bus rate. Pull-up values follow from the SCL frequency and the bus capacitance.

operation.topic: TWI bus interface and address match
operation.text: TWDR holds the byte to send or the byte received; a separate (N)ACK bit is set through TWCR when receiving and read from TWSR when transmitting. The START/STOP controller detects START and STOP even in sleep, and the address match unit compares received addresses with TWAR (and the general call if TWGCE is set) in sleep too, so the part wakes when addressed. If another interrupt wakes the CPU during a Power-down address match, the TWI aborts and goes idle; making the address match the only enabled interrupt in Power-down avoids this.

When a bus event needs the application, TWINT sets and TWSR takes a status code in the next clock; at other times TWSR reads a code meaning no status is available. SCL is held low while TWINT is set. TWINT sets after a START or REPEATED START is sent, after SLA+R/W, after an address byte, after lost arbitration, when addressed by its own address or the general call, after a data byte is received, after a STOP or REPEATED START while still addressed as slave, and on a bus error from an illegal START or STOP.

The TWI is byte oriented and interrupt driven. With TWIE and the global interrupt flag set, TWINT raises an interrupt; otherwise software polls TWINT. While TWINT is set the application reads TWSR, loads TWDR for the next cycle, then writes TWCR with TWINT written to one, which clears the flag and starts the next operation; the TWI does nothing while TWINT is set. A master write of one byte runs: write TWCR to send START; wait for TWINT and check for status START; load SLA+W, clear TWINT; wait and check that SLA+W was acknowledged; load the data, clear TWINT; wait and check that the data was acknowledged; write TWCR to send STOP. TWINT does not set after a STOP. Status is read with the prescaler bits masked (TWSR & 0xF8).

Four modes, MT and MR (master sending or receiving) and ST and SR (slave sending or receiving), used together as the application needs, for example MT to write an EEPROM and MR to read it back. A master mode is entered by sending START; sending SLA+W then gives MT and SLA+R gives MR. Status codes assume the prescaler bits are zero or masked.

After START, load SLA+W into TWDR and clear TWINT. Once SLA+W is sent and the acknowledge received, TWSR reads 0x18, 0x20 or 0x38. Each data byte is loaded into TWDR while TWINT is high and sent by clearing TWINT, until STOP or a REPEATED START ends the transfer. After a REPEATED START (0x10) the master can address the same or another slave, or switch between transmitter and receiver, without releasing the bus.

After START, load SLA+R and clear TWINT. Once SLA+R is sent and the acknowledge received, TWSR reads 0x38, 0x40 or 0x48. Received bytes are read from TWDR while TWINT is set. After the last byte the master returns a NACK, then sends STOP or a REPEATED START; the TWCR values for START, continuing, STOP and REPEATED START are the same as in master transmitter mode.

Load TWAR with the own 7-bit address in its upper bits (LSB = 1 also answers the general call, address 0x00) and set TWCR with TWEN and TWEA one and TWSTA and TWSTO zero. The TWI then waits for its address (or the general call); a write bit gives SR mode and a read bit ST mode, and TWINT sets with a status code. SR mode can also follow lost arbitration as master (0x68, 0x78). Clearing TWEA during a transfer returns NOT ACK after the next byte; while TWEA is zero the own address is not acknowledged, though the bus is still watched, so TWEA can isolate the TWI for a while.

In every sleep mode except Idle the TWI clock is off, but with TWEA set the interface still acknowledges its own address or the general call, clocked from SCL, and wakes the part; SCL is held low through the wake until TWINT is cleared, so a long start-up time can block the bus for that long. After such a wake TWDR does not hold the last byte seen on the bus.

Set up TWAR and TWCR as for slave receiver; the own address with a read bit gives ST mode, as can lost arbitration as master (0xB0). If TWEA is cleared during the transfer the TWI sends its last byte and moves to 0xC0 (master answered NACK) or 0xC8 (master answered ACK and wants more), then becomes a not addressed slave and ignores the master, which reads all ones. As in slave receiver mode, TWEA = 0 stops address recognition while the bus is still watched, and the part can wake from sleep on its own address with SCL held low until TWINT is cleared.

0xF8: no status available, TWINT = 0; this shows between states and when the TWI is not in a transfer. 0x00: bus error, a START or STOP in an illegal place such as during an address, data or acknowledge bit; TWINT sets. To recover, set TWSTO and clear TWINT: the TWI enters not addressed slave mode, clears TWSTO, releases SDA and SCL and sends no STOP.

Reading a serial EEPROM needs MT mode to send the address to read and MR mode to read the data, with the direction change made by a REPEATED START between them (START, SLA+W, address, REPEATED START, SLA+R, data, STOP), so the master keeps the bus and no other master can move the EEPROM's pointer in between.

Masters sending identical transfers to the same slave never notice each other. Masters addressing one slave but differing in data or direction lose arbitration in the R/W bit or the data, and losers go to not addressed slave mode or wait for a free bus to send START, as software decides. Masters addressing different slaves lose in the SLA bits; a loser checks whether the winner addressed it and enters SR or ST mode if so, otherwise it goes to not addressed slave mode or waits to send START. Status codes after lost arbitration: 0x38 (lost in data, or in SLA without being addressed), 0x68 or 0x78 (addressed for write, by own address or general call) and 0xB0 (addressed for read).

Compares the positive input AIN0 with the negative input AIN1 and sets the output ACO when AIN0 is higher. The output can trigger Timer/Counter1 input capture and has its own interrupt on a rising, falling or either edge. The positive input can be replaced by the fixed bandgap reference (ACBG), which needs time to settle before its first use. PRADC in PRR0 must be zero to use the ADC multiplexer as the comparator input.

Any of ADC15:0 can replace AIN1 as the negative input: with ACME in ADCSRB set and the ADC off (ADEN = 0), MUX5 and MUX2:0 in ADMUX pick the pin. With ACME clear or ADEN set, AIN1 is used. Writing ACD in ACSR powers the comparator off to save current in Active and Idle; clear ACIE first, or changing ACD can raise an interrupt.

A 10-bit successive approximation ADC behind an analog multiplexer of 8 or 16 single-ended inputs from Port F and Port K, referred to GND. It supports 16 or 32 differential input combinations. Four pairs (ADC1 and ADC0, ADC3 and ADC2, ADC9 and ADC8, ADC11 and ADC10) have a gain stage of 1× (0 dB), 10× (20 dB) or 200× (46 dB). The 16 channels form two groups of 8, each with a common negative input (ADC1 or ADC9) for seven differential channels whose positive input is any other pin of the group. Expect 8-bit resolution at 1× or 10× and 7-bit at 200×. A sample and hold keeps the input steady during conversion. AVCC, the analog supply, must stay within ±0.3 V of VCC. Internal references of 1.1 V, 2.56 V or AVCC are available, and AREF can take a decoupling capacitor. PRADC in PRR0 must be zero.

The lowest code is GND and the highest is the AREF voltage minus 1 LSB. REFSn in ADMUX connects AVCC, 1.1 V or 2.56 V to AREF. MUX bits in ADMUX and ADCSRB choose any input pin, GND or the fixed bandgap as single-ended inputs, or a pair through the differential amplifier (bypassed for single-ended). ADEN in ADCSRA enables the ADC; reference and channel take effect only then, and the ADC draws no power with ADEN clear, so switch it off before power-saving sleep. The result sits in ADCH:ADCL, right adjusted unless ADLAR is set. With left adjustment and 8 bits enough, read only ADCH; otherwise read ADCL then ADCH. Reading ADCL locks both registers until ADCH is read, and a conversion finishing in between is lost, though its interrupt still fires.

Writing ADSC to one starts a single conversion; ADSC stays high until it ends, and a channel change during a conversion waits for it to finish. With ADATE set, a rising edge on the source chosen by ADTS in ADCSRB resets the prescaler and starts a conversion, for conversions at fixed intervals; an edge during a conversion, or a trigger still high at its end, starts nothing new. The interrupt flag sets even with the interrupt disabled, and must be cleared before the next trigger. Using ADIF as the trigger gives free running mode, where each conversion starts the next regardless of ADIF; the first is started by ADSC. ADSC reads one during any conversion.

For full 10-bit resolution the ADC clock must be 50 kHz to 200 kHz; for less resolution it can go up to 1000 kHz. The 7-bit prescaler (ADPS in ADCSRA: CK/2 to CK/128) derives it from any CPU clock above 100 kHz, runs while ADEN is set and is held reset while ADEN is low. A single conversion starts at the next rising ADC clock edge after ADSC. A normal conversion takes 13 ADC clocks; the first after ADEN is set takes 25 to initialize the analog circuits. Sample and hold is 1.5 ADC clocks into a normal conversion and 13.5 into a first one; at the end the result is written and ADIF set (ADSC clears in single conversion mode). With auto triggering, sample and hold is 2 ADC clocks after the trigger edge, plus three CPU clocks of synchronization. Free running starts the next conversion at once while ADSC stays high. After selecting the bandgap as input, the first reading may be wrong until it settles.

Differential conversions are synchronized to CKADC2, half the ADC clock. A conversion started by the user while CKADC2 is low takes 13 ADC clocks, while high 14; free running conversions after the first take 14. With auto triggering the prescaler reset spoils the gain stage's clock, so the ADC must be switched off and on between differential conversions (ADEN to 0, then 1), giving valid extended conversions.

MUXn and REFS1:0 pass through a temporary register; the selection follows writes until a conversion starts, is then locked, and follows again from the last ADC clock before the conversion ends. Wait one ADC clock after writing ADSC before changing ADMUX. With ADATE and ADEN both set a trigger can come at any time; change ADMUX only with ADATE or ADEN clear, at least one ADC clock after a trigger during a conversion, or after a conversion before its trigger flag is cleared, and the change applies to the next conversion. A new differential channel can take up to 125 µs to settle; do not convert in that time or discard those results, and allow the same after a reference change before a differential conversion.

In single conversion mode select the channel before starting, or change it one ADC clock after ADSC; waiting for the conversion to end is simplest. In free running mode select it before the first conversion; a change made after that shows one result late, since the next conversion has already begun. The first result after switching to a differential gain channel may be inaccurate while the offset cancellation settles and is best discarded.

VREF sets the conversion range; single-ended inputs above it read close to 0x3FF. It can be AVCC (through a passive switch), the internal 1.1 V reference (the bandgap VBG through an amplifier), the internal 2.56 V reference (made from the 1.1 V one) or an external voltage on AREF. AREF connects straight to the ADC, so a capacitor from AREF to ground reduces noise and VREF can be measured there with a high impedance meter; it is a high impedance source and should carry only a capacitive load. With an external voltage on AREF the internal options must not be used, as they would be shorted to it; with nothing on AREF the user can switch between AVCC, 1.1 V and 2.56 V. Discard the first result after a reference change. For differential channels the reference must stay the margin from AVCC given in the ADC characteristics.

Conversions can run in ADC Noise Reduction or Idle sleep to keep out CPU and I/O noise: with the ADC enabled, idle, in single conversion mode and its interrupt enabled, enter the sleep mode; the conversion starts once the CPU halts, and its interrupt wakes the CPU. If another interrupt wakes the CPU first, that runs and the ADC interrupt follows when the conversion ends; the CPU stays awake until the next SLEEP. In other sleep modes the ADC is not switched off automatically, so clear ADEN first; for differential conversions after such a wake, switch the ADC off and on to force an extended conversion.

Each ADCn pin presents its capacitance and leakage whether or not it is selected; once selected, the source charges the 14 pF sample and hold capacitor through a series resistance of 1 to 100 kΩ. Sources of about 10 kΩ or less make the sampling time negligible; higher impedances need longer, which varies widely, so slow signals from low impedance sources are best. No signal content above the Nyquist frequency (fADC/2) should be present on any channel; filter it out first.

Keep analog tracks short, over the ground plane and away from fast digital lines; supply AVCC from VCC through an LC filter; use the noise canceler; and do not switch ADC port pins used as digital outputs while a conversion runs.

The gain stage nulls most of the differential offset itself. The remainder can be measured by selecting the same pin for both differential inputs and subtracted in software, bringing the offset of any channel below one LSB.

An IEEE 1149.1 test access port serves three jobs: board test by boundary scan, programming the Flash, EEPROM, fuses and lock bits, and on-chip debugging. Through it a debugger reaches every peripheral, internal and external RAM, the register file, the program counter and the non-volatile memories, and can stop the CPU on a BREAK instruction, a change of program flow, a single step, or a program or data address (single address or range). A 4-bit instruction register selects which data register sits between TDI and TDO: the ID, bypass and boundary-scan registers for board test, the programming registers, and the internal and break point scan chains, which only debugging uses. The debug instructions are private and given only to selected tool vendors.

Four pins form the port: TMS steers the TAP state machine, TCK clocks every JTAG operation, TDI carries serial data into the instruction or data register, and TDO carries it out. The optional TRST reset pin does not exist. With the JTAGEN fuse unprogrammed the four pins are ordinary port pins and the TAP controller is held in reset; with it programmed the TAP inputs get internal pull-ups and JTAG works for boundary scan and programming. Parts leave the factory with JTAGEN programmed. For debugging, the debugger also watches R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ to see external resets and may drive it low to reset the system, which needs every other driver on that line to be open collector.

A 16-state machine moves on each rising TCK edge according to TMS; after power-on reset it sits in Test-Logic-Reset. Every shift register shifts least significant bit first. From Run-Test/Idle, TMS = 1, 1, 0, 0 reaches Shift-IR; the 4-bit instruction is then shifted in on TDI with TMS low for the first three bits and high for the last, which also leaves the state, while TDO returns the captured value 0x01. TMS = 1, 1, 0 goes back to Run-Test/Idle, latching the instruction in Update-IR. TMS = 1, 0, 0 from Run-Test/Idle reaches Shift-DR, where the selected data register shifts with TMS low until its last bit, TDO returning what Capture-DR loaded; 1, 1, 0 returns to Run-Test/Idle, with any latched output updated in Update-DR. The Exit, Pause and Exit2 states are for moving round the machine only. Run-Test/Idle need not be visited between instruction and data, and some instructions act in it. Holding TMS high for five TCK periods reaches Test-Logic-Reset from any state.

Debugging uses a scan chain between the CPU and the peripherals, a break point unit, and a channel between CPU and JTAG. The debugger feeds AVR instructions to the CPU through the scan chain, and the CPU posts results to an I/O location that belongs to that channel. The break point unit gives break on program-flow change, single step, and four break points (two program-memory and two combined) that can be arranged in the combinations listed below; a debugger may keep some of them for itself. Debugging needs JTAGEN and OCDEN programmed and no lock bits set: setting LB1 or LB2 turns the debug system off, so a locked part cannot be read through it. A debugger can offer any number of code break points through the BREAK instruction plus up to two data break points or one masked range.

Programming over JTAG needs only TCK, TMS, TDI and TDO besides power, and no 12 V. It needs JTAGEN programmed and MCUCR's JTD bit at 0. Flash, EEPROM, fuses and lock bits can all be written and verified, with the same lock-bit protection as parallel programming. Once LB1 or LB2 is programmed, OCDEN cannot be programmed without a chip erase first, so a secured part cannot be opened for debug.

OCDR at I/O address 0x31 (data address 0x51) passes bytes from the running program to the debugger. A CPU write sets the internal flag IDRD; a CPU read returns the seven low bits of OCDR with IDRD as the top bit, and the debugger clears IDRD once it has read the byte. Where OCDR shares its address with an ordinary I/O register, OCDR is reached only with OCDEN programmed and the debugger enabling it; otherwise the ordinary register is accessed.

The boundary-scan chain can drive and observe every digital I/O pin and the digital-to-analog boundary of analog circuits with pins. On a board all JTAG parts are chained TDI to TDO; a tester sets outputs, reads inputs and compares them with what it expects, testing the board's connections with only the four TAP signals. The mandatory IDCODE, BYPASS, SAMPLE/PRELOAD and EXTEST instructions and the AVR-specific AVR_RESET serve board test. IDCODE is the default instruction, so the first data scan returns the device ID. The CPU may be held in reset during test; if it is not, scans may set its inputs and leave its program in an unknown state on exit; in reset every port output goes high impedance at once, which is why HIGHZ is not needed. Reset comes from pulling R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ low or from AVR_RESET with the reset register set. EXTEST drives the output latches onto the pins the moment it is loaded, so SAMPLE/PRELOAD should set safe values first; SAMPLE/PRELOAD also snapshots the pins while the part runs. JTAGEN programmed and JTD in MCUCR cleared enable the port. For boundary scan TCK may run faster than the chip clock, and the chip clock need not run at all.

Four data registers serve boundary scan: bypass, device identification, reset and the boundary-scan chain. The bypass register is one stage, cleared on leaving Capture-DR, and shortens the chain while other parts are tested. The 32-bit ID register holds a version (the device revision: A = 0x0, B = 0x1 and so on), a 16-bit part number and the 11-bit manufacturer ID, with bit 0 fixed at 1. The one-bit reset register holds the part in reset while it holds a 1, exactly as R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ low would; its output is not latched, so reset starts at once, and on release the part stays in reset for the time-out its clock fuses select. Because port pins go high impedance in reset, this register also stands in for the missing HIGHZ instruction.

Each bidirectional pin has a cell that folds output control (OC), output data (OD) and input data (ID) into a two-stage shift register; FF0 holds a pin's data bit and FF1 its control bit. Pull-ups are off while the instruction register holds EXTEST or SAMPLE_PRELOAD. With no alternate function, ID is the PINxn value without its synchronizer, OD is PORTxn, OC is DDxn, and the pull-up enable is the AND of PUD inverted, DDxn inverted and PORTxn. Digital alternate functions connect outside the scan cell, so the chain reads the real pin. Analog functions connect straight to the pin with no scan cell between digital and analog, but some digital controls of the analog blocks are turned off to avoid contention on the pads.
With EXTEST or SAMPLE_PRELOAD in the instruction register, the system clock does not reach the CLKO pin even with CKOUT programmed, and the scan never samples the clock.
R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ takes 5 V active-low logic for reset and 12 V active-high when entering high-voltage parallel programming. The 5 V reset signal has an observe-only scan cell (RSTT).

JTD, bit 7 of MCUCR (I/O 0x35, data 0x55), turns the JTAG interface off when 1; at 0 the interface is on if JTAGEN is programmed. To change it, software writes the new value twice within four cycles. JTD must stay unchanged while the on-chip debugger is in use. JTRF, bit 4 of MCUSR (I/O 0x34, data 0x54), is set by a reset from a 1 in the JTAG reset register under AVR_RESET; power-on reset or writing 0 clears it.

Bit 0 is the first bit shifted in and out. The order follows the pinout where it can, so Port A and Port K run in reverse bit order against the other ports; the scan chains of the analog circuits take the most significant bits whatever pins they connect to. PF4 to PF7 are absent from the chain, being the TAP pins while JTAG is on. BSDL files describing the chain exist for the ATmega1281/2561 and for the ATmega640/1280/2560.

Code running from a boot loader section in Flash can read and write the whole Flash, its own section included, while the CPU keeps running: the part can fetch new code over any interface and protocol and program it, change the boot loader itself, or erase it when it is no longer wanted. The boot section's size is set by fuses, and two independent sets of boot lock bits protect it and the application section. A separate fuse points the reset vector at the boot loader. Flash is written a page at a time; this grouping into pages matters only for programming, not for normal running.

Flash splits into an application section and a boot loader section (BLS), sized by the BOOTSZ fuses and each with its own lock bits (boot lock bits 0 for the application, boot lock bits 1 for the BLS). SPM starts a write only when it runs from the BLS, so the boot loader must live there; from the application section SPM is disabled. From the BLS, SPM reaches all of Flash.

Independently of the BOOTSZ split, Flash has two fixed parts, RWW (read-while-write) and NRWW (no read-while-write). Erasing or writing a page in RWW lets the CPU go on running code from NRWW; erasing or writing a page in NRWW halts the CPU for the whole operation. The names refer to the section being programmed. While RWW is busy, no code in it may be fetched, by LPM, call, jump or interrupt, or the program may end in an unknown state; disable interrupts or move the vectors into the BLS, which always lies in NRWW.
