RWWSB in SPMCSR reads 1 while RWW is blocked, and software must clear it after programming before using RWW code.

With no boot loader the whole Flash holds application code. The two sets of boot lock bits let software updates be blocked for the whole Flash, for the BLS only, for the application section only, or for neither. They can be set by software and by serial or parallel programming but cleared only by chip erase. The general lock modes (LB) do not govern SPM writes or (E)LPM reads.

The application enters the boot loader by a jump or call, for instance on a command arriving over the USART or SPI. Or BOOTRST is programmed so that reset starts at the boot loader's first address, and the boot loader later hands over to the application. The CPU cannot change its own fuses, so once BOOTRST is programmed only serial or parallel programming can change it back.

SPM takes its address from the Z-pointer: ZL and ZH (R30 and R31) plus RAMPZ in I/O space, which exists only when program memory exceeds 64 Kbytes and supplies Z bits 23:16. The low address bits pick the word within a page (PCWORD) and the high bits that page (PCPAGE). Page erase and page write are addressed separately, so the boot loader must give both the same page. Once an operation starts the address is latched and Z is free. (E)LPM addresses Flash by byte, so it also uses Z0.

Flash is updated page by page, and a page must be erased before the temporary page buffer is written into it. The buffer, filled one word at a time by SPM in any order, can be loaded before a page erase (then the old page can be read, changed and written back, a read-modify-write) or between erase and write (then the old data is gone). Any part of that page that is to stay must be saved before the erase and rewritten. Erase and write must address the same page.

Each SPM operation is started by writing SPMCSR and executing SPM within four clock cycles. Page erase: page address in PCPAGE of Z, SPMCSR = X0000011, R1:R0 ignored, other Z bits ignored. Page load: word address in PCWORD of Z, data in R1:R0, SPMCSR = 00000001; the buffer clears itself after a page write, on writing RWWSRE, and on system reset, and each address can be written only once between clears. An EEPROM write during page loading leaves the loaded data intact. Page write: page address in PCPAGE, other Z bits zero, SPMCSR = X0000101, R1:R0 ignored. An erase or write in RWW lets NRWW code run; in NRWW the CPU halts.

With the SPM interrupt enabled, an interrupt is requested continuously while SPMEN in SPMCSR is clear, so it can replace polling. The interrupt vectors should then sit in the BLS so that no interrupt fetches from a blocked RWW section.

Leaving boot lock bit 11 unprogrammed lets the BLS be rewritten, and an accidental write can wreck the boot loader and end further updates. Where the boot loader never needs changing, programming BLB11 guards it against internal writes.

RWW cannot be read during page erase or page write, and software must keep from addressing it; RWWSB stays 1 while it is busy. Move the vector table into the BLS or disable interrupts. After programming, write RWWSRE to clear RWWSB before using RWW again.

Put the lock values in R0, write X0001001 to SPMCSR and run SPM within four cycles. A 0 in any of R0 bits 5:0 programs that lock bit. Z is don't care, though 0x0001 (the lock-bit read address) and 1s in R0 bits 7 and 6 are advised for future parts. All of Flash stays readable while lock bits are written.
While an EEPROM write runs, every software write to Flash is blocked, and so are software reads of fuses and lock bits. Check that EEPE in EECR is clear before writing SPMCSR.

operation.topic: Reading fuse and lock bits from software
operation.text: Load Z with the byte's address, set BLBSET and SPMEN in SPMCSR, and execute (E)LPM within three CPU cycles: the destination register receives the lock bits (Z = 0x0001), fuse low byte (0x0000), fuse high byte (0x0003) or extended fuse byte (0x0002). BLBSET and SPMEN clear themselves when the read completes, or when no (E)LPM follows within three cycles or no SPM within four, after which (E)LPM behaves normally. A programmed bit reads 0 and an unprogrammed bit 1.

operation.topic: Reading the signature row from software
operation.text: Load Z with the signature byte's address, set SIGRD and SPMEN in SPMCSR and execute LPM within three CPU cycles to get the byte. SIGRD and SPMEN clear themselves when the read completes or when no LPM follows within three cycles.

A supply too low for the CPU and Flash can corrupt program memory in two ways: a Flash write needs a minimum voltage to complete correctly, and the CPU can misexecute instructions. Any one of these avoids it: program the boot lock bits when the boot loader never needs updating; hold R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ low while the supply is short, with the brown-out detector if its level suits, or an external supervisor (a write under way when reset arrives still finishes if the supply allows); or keep the core in power-down sleep through low-supply periods so it cannot execute stray SPM writes.
Flash write timing comes from the calibrated RC oscillator.

The example routine copies one page from RAM (Y-pointer) to Flash (Z-pointer) and must run from the boot section, with interrupts disabled or the vectors moved there. It erases that page, re-enables RWW, loads the buffer a word at a time with SPMEN, writes that page, re-enables RWW, optionally reads that page back with ELPM and compares, and before returning loops until RWWSB reads 0, re-enabling RWW as needed. Its SPM helper waits for SPMEN to clear, saves SREG and disables interrupts, waits for EEPE to clear, writes SPMCSR, executes SPM and restores SREG.
Six lock bits, each unprogrammed (1) or programmed (0), add the protections below. Only chip erase returns them to 1. LB1 and LB2 go in last, after the fuses and boot lock bits.

Three fuse bytes; a programmed fuse reads 0. Chip erase leaves the fuses alone, and programming LB1 locks them, so fuses go in before lock bits. Fuse values latch on entering programming mode and changes act only after leaving it, except EESAVE, which acts as soon as it is programmed. In normal mode the fuses latch at power-up. OCDEN must never be left programmed in a shipped product, whatever the lock bits and JTAGEN: it keeps parts of the clock system running in every sleep mode and can raise the supply current.

A three-byte signature in its own address space identifies the device and can be read in serial and parallel mode even when the part is locked. The high byte of address 0x000 in that space holds the internal RC oscillator's calibration value, copied into OSCCAL at every reset.

In parallel programming several pins take programming names (pin name mapping below); the rest keep their own names. Pulses are 250 ns or longer unless stated otherwise. A positive pulse on XTAL1 does what XA1:XA0 select; a pulse on W̅R̅ or O̅E̅ acts on the command last loaded. Pins not used should be left floating.

Apply 4.5 V to 5.5 V between VCC and GND. With R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ at 0, give XTAL1 six or more toggles. Put PAGEL, XA1, XA0 and BS1 (the Prog_enable pins) at 0000 and wait at least 100 ns. Raise R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ to 11.5 V to 12.5 V; any change on the Prog_enable pins within 100 ns of that makes entry fail. Wait at least 50 µs before the first command.

Command and address stay loaded during programming. Load the command once for a run of reads or writes; skip writing 0xFF, which is what Flash and EEPROM (unless EESAVE is programmed) hold after chip erase; and reload the address high byte only when moving to a new 256-word Flash or 256-byte EEPROM window, signature reads included.

Chip erase clears Flash and EEPROM (EEPROM survives if EESAVE is programmed) and the lock bits, the lock bits only after program memory is fully erased; fuses are untouched. Flash or EEPROM must be chip-erased before reprogramming. Sequence: XA1:XA0 = 10, BS1 = 0, DATA = 1000 0000, positive pulse on XTAL1 to load the command, then a negative pulse on W̅R̅ starts the erase; RDY/B̅S̅Y̅ goes low and a new command waits until it is high again.

Data collects in a page buffer and a whole page is written at once. Steps: (A) load command 0001 0000 with XA1:XA0 = 10, BS1 = 0 and an XTAL1 pulse; (B) address low byte with XA1:XA0 = 00, BS2:BS1 = 00; (C) data low byte with XA1:XA0 = 01; (D) data high byte with BS1 = 1, XA1:XA0 = 01; (E) with BS1 = 1, a positive PAGEL pulse latches the word; (F) repeat B to E until the buffer is full or that page's data is in. The low address bits pick the word in that page and the high bits that page; with fewer than 256 words per page the top bits of the low address byte take part in choosing that page. (G) address high byte with BS2:BS1 = 01; (H) address extended high byte (bits 23:16) with BS2:BS1 = 10; (I) with BS2:BS1 = 00 a negative W̅R̅ pulse writes that page, RDY/B̅S̅Y̅ goes low and the next step waits for it to go high; (J) repeat B to I for all data; (K) end with command 0000 0000 (no operation) loaded by an XTAL1 pulse, which resets the internal write signals.

EEPROM is written through a page buffer too: load command 0001 0001 (A), address high byte (G), address low byte (B), data (C), latch with a PAGEL pulse (E), repeating B to E until the buffer is full; then with BS2:BS1 = 00 a negative W̅R̅ pulse writes that page, and the next page waits until RDY/B̅S̅Y̅ goes high.

operation.topic: Parallel reading of Flash and EEPROM
operation.text: Flash: load command 0000 0010, then the extended, high and low address bytes; with O̅E̅ = 0 and BS1 = 0 DATA shows the word's low byte, with BS1 = 1 its high byte; then O̅E̅ = 1. EEPROM: load command 0000 0011, the high and low address bytes, then O̅E̅ = 0 and BS1 = 0 to read the byte, and O̅E̅ = 1.

Fuses: load command 0100 0000 and the data low byte, where a 0 bit programs and a 1 bit erases the fuse. With BS2:BS1 = 00 a W̅R̅ pulse writes the low fuse byte; with BS2:BS1 = 01 the high byte; with 10 the extended byte; each write waits for RDY/B̅S̅Y̅ high, and BS2:BS1 return to 00 after. Lock bits: load command 0010 0000 and the data low byte (a 0 bit programs that lock bit), pulse W̅R̅ and wait for RDY/B̅S̅Y̅. With LB mode 3 in place the boot lock bits cannot be programmed by any external mode. Only chip erase clears lock bits.

operation.topic: Parallel reading of fuses, lock bits, signature and calibration
operation.text: Load command 0000 0100; with O̅E̅ = 0, BS2:BS1 = 00 shows the fuse low byte, 11 the fuse high byte, 10 the extended fuse byte and 01 the lock bits, a 0 meaning programmed; then O̅E̅ = 1. Signature: command 0000 1000, address low byte 0x00 to 0x02, O̅E̅ = 0 with BS1 = 0 reads the byte. Calibration: the same command, address 0x00, O̅E̅ = 0 with BS1 = 1.

Flash and EEPROM can be programmed over a three-wire serial bus (SCK, PDI in, PDO out) while R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ is held at GND. After R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ goes low, the Programming Enable instruction must come first. On some packages the serial programming pins are not the SPI peripheral's pins (pin mapping below). EEPROM writes in serial mode erase the byte themselves, so no chip erase is needed first; chip erase sets every Flash and EEPROM location to 0xFF. AVCC must stay within VCC ± 0.3 V and within 1.8 V to 5.5 V. A valid clock to suit the CKSEL fuses must be present; on the internal oscillator XTAL1 needs no clock.

Data in is taken on the rising SCK edge and data out changes on the falling edge. Power up with R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ and SCK at 0; if the programmer cannot hold SCK low during power-up, pulse R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ high for at least two CPU clocks after SCK is at 0. Wait at least 20 ms, then send Programming Enable on PDI. When in step, the second byte (0x53) echoes back while the third byte goes out; all four bytes are sent either way, and without the echo R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ gets a positive pulse and Programming Enable is sent again. Flash is written a page at a time: each byte goes into its page buffer with the 7 low address bits through Load Program Memory Page, low byte before high byte at each address, and Write Program Memory Page with address bits 15:8 stores that page. Load Extended Address Byte sets the address MSB beforehand; it is kept until sent again, so it is needed for the first page and on crossing each 64K-word boundary. Without polling, wait tWD_FLASH before the next page; touching the interface before the write ends can corrupt it. EEPROM is written a byte at a time with address and data, each location erasing itself first; without polling wait tWD_EEPROM between bytes; on an erased part 0xFF bytes can be skipped. Read instructions return any location on PDO; Flash reads take the upper address byte from Load Extended Address Byte. At the end, R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ high starts normal running; to power off, set R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ to 1 and then remove VCC.

operation.topic: Serial programming polling and page loading
operation.text: When the LSB of the Poll RDY/B̅S̅Y̅ response is 1 a programming operation is still running; wait for 0 before the next instruction. Within a page the low data byte is loaded before the high byte. Once its page buffer is loaded, the EEPROM page is written with Write EEPROM Memory Page.

JTAG programming uses TCK, TMS, TDI and TDO only, with no control of the reset or clock pins. JTAGEN must be programmed (it is at delivery) and JTD in MCUCR cleared. Or, with JTD set, holding external reset low clears JTD after two chip clocks and frees the JTAG pins for programming, so the pins can serve as ordinary ports while running and still allow in-system programming. That trick does not work for boundary scan or debugging, which need the pins kept for JTAG. TCK must stay below the chip's maximum frequency while programming, and the system clock prescaler cannot be used to bring it low enough. Shift registers shift least significant bit first.
The 4-bit instruction register holds up to 16 instructions. The TAP's Run-Test/Idle state generates internal clocks and also serves as an idle state between JTAG sequences.

operation.topic: JTAG page load and page read
operation.text: Under PROG_PAGELOAD each Update-DR writes one byte into its page buffer, alternating low byte then high byte, starting with the low byte. The program counter steps forward before each low byte except the first, so the first byte lands at the address PROG_COMMANDS set and the last byte of that page leaves the counter inside that page. Under PROG_PAGEREAD each Capture-DR reads one byte, alternating low then high starting with low; the counter steps after every high byte, the first included, so reading starts at the set address and the last byte of a page moves the counter into the next page.

Four data registers serve programming: reset, programming enable, programming command and Flash data byte. The part must be reset through the reset register before entering programming mode; a 1 holds it in reset like R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ low, with no latch, and on release the clock fuses' time-out applies. The 16-bit programming enable register enables JTAG programming when it holds the signature 0b1010_0011_0111_0000 (0xA370); power-on reset clears it, and it should be cleared on leaving programming mode. The 15-bit programming command register shifts commands in and the previous command's result out.

This register is an 8-bit scan chain plus an 8-bit holding register, run by a TCK-clocked state machine that drives the Flash control lines and watches its strobes, so only data needs shifting to fill its page buffer before a page write or to read Flash back. During page load each Update-DR copies the chain to the holding register and starts a write into its page buffer that takes up to 11 TCK cycles. Shifting eight bits per byte gives the state machine enough clocks from the TAP moves alone; with fewer bits between Update-DR states, stay in Run-Test/Idle so that at least 11 TCK cycles separate them.

Steps refer to the rows of the JTAG programming instruction set. Enter: AVR_RESET with a 1 in the reset register, then PROG_ENABLE with 0b1010_0011_0111_0000 in the enable register. Leave: PROG_COMMANDS, no-operation command 11a, PROG_ENABLE with all zeros, then AVR_RESET with a 0. Chip erase: PROG_COMMANDS, 1a, then poll with 1b or wait tWLRH_CE.

Flash must be chip-erased first. Word by word: PROG_COMMANDS, 2a, then 2b, 2c and 2d for the address, 2e, 2f and 2g for each word (repeating 2d onward through that page), 2h to write that page, and 2i or a wait of tWLRH; repeat from 2b for every page. Faster: after 2a and its page address (2b to 2d with PCWORD = 0), switch to PROG_PAGELOAD and shift the whole page in byte by byte, LSB of the first word first and MSB of the last word last, Update-DR placing each byte and advancing the counter; then PROG_COMMANDS, 2h, and 2i or tWLRH. Reading: PROG_COMMANDS, 3a, address with 3b to 3d, data with 3e, repeating per word; or after its page address switch to PROG_PAGEREAD and shift out that page or the whole Flash, LSB of the first word first. Capture-DR both reads and advances, and it comes before Shift-DR, so the first byte out is valid; return to PROG_COMMANDS for each new address.

operation.topic: JTAG EEPROM, fuse and lock programming
operation.text: EEPROM must be chip-erased first: PROG_COMMANDS, 4a, address high (4b) and low (4c) bytes, data with 4d and 4e for each byte of that page, 4f to write, 4g or tWLRH. Reading: 5a, 5b and 5c, then 5d per byte. PROG_PAGELOAD and PROG_PAGEREAD do not work for EEPROM. Fuses: PROG_COMMANDS, 6a, then for each fuse byte load its data (0 programs, 1 unprograms), write it and poll, or wait tWLRH. Lock bits: 7a, data with 7b (0 programs, 1 leaves unchanged), 7c to write, 7d or tWLRH.

operation.topic: JTAG reading fuses, lock bits, signature and calibration
operation.text: Fuses and lock bits: PROG_COMMANDS, 8a, then the read sequence for one byte or 8f for all of them. Signature: PROG_COMMANDS, 9a, then 9b with address 0x00 and 9c for the first byte, and the same with 0x01 and 0x02 for the second and third. Calibration: PROG_COMMANDS, 10a, 10b with address 0x00, and 10c.

The highest clock frequency depends on VCC and rises linearly between 1.8 V and 2.7 V and between 2.7 V and 4.5 V. V devices (ATmega640V/1280V/1281V/2560V/2561V): 4 MHz at 1.8 V up to 8 MHz at 2.7 V, then 8 MHz to 5.5 V. ATmega2560V/2561V running from the No-Read-While-Write section as well: 2 MHz at 1.8 V up to 8 MHz at 2.7 V, then 8 MHz to 5.5 V; code that runs only in the Read-While-Write section reaches the higher speed at low voltage. 16 MHz ATmega640/1280/1281: 8 MHz at 2.7 V up to 16 MHz at 4.5 V, then 16 MHz to 5.5 V. 16 MHz ATmega2560/2561: 16 MHz from 4.5 V to 5.5 V.
The external clock on XTAL1 is timed between its crossings of VIL1 and VIH1: high time tCHCX, low time tCLCX, rise time tCLCH, fall time tCHCL and period tCLCL.

Two power-on reset circuits exist. The standard one is in the early silicon: ATmega640, ATmega1280 and ATmega1281 revision A, and ATmega2560 and ATmega2561 revisions A to E. The enhanced one is in ATmega640, ATmega1280 and ATmega1281 revision B and later, and ATmega2560 and ATmega2561 revision F and later.

The bus timing symbols are measured on SCL and SDA as follows: tSU;STA from SCL high to SDA falling for a (repeated) start, tHD;STA from SDA falling to SCL falling, tLOW and tHIGH the SCL low and high periods, tHD;DAT and tSU;DAT the SDA hold after and setup before the SCL edges, tSU;STO from SCL rising to SDA rising for a stop, tBUF the idle time between a stop and the next start, tof the fall time and tr the rise time.

Master mode: MOSI output is valid (6) before the first SCK edge; the SCK period is (1) and its high and low times (2) for either CPOL; MISO input is set up (4) and held (5) around the sampling edge; MOSI output changes (7) after the shifting edge, and (8) after the last edge; (3) is the rise and fall time. Slave mode: MISO output is valid (9) after S̅S̅ falls; SCK period (10) and high and low times (11); MOSI input set up (13) and held (14); MISO changes (15) after the shifting edge; S̅S̅ may rise (16) after the last SCK edge and MISO goes to high impedance (17) after it; (18) is from S̅S̅ low to the first SCK edge; (12) is the rise and fall time.

An external memory access with no wait state takes system clock cycles T1 to T3, with a fourth cycle T4 for the next ALE. ALE pulses high in T1 (1) and the low address byte on DA7:0 and the high byte on A15:8 are valid before ALE falls (2, 4) and held after it (3a write, 3b read). For a write, W̅R̅ falls (6, 7) once the address is valid, data is set up (13) before W̅R̅ falls and is valid (15) until W̅R̅ rises, held (14) after it; the W̅R̅ pulse is (16). For a read with XMBK = 0, R̅D̅ falls (5, 8), data is valid (10) after it falls, set up (9) before it rises and held (11) after; the R̅D̅ pulse is (12). SRWn1:0 = 01 adds one wait cycle (T1 to T5), 10 adds two (T1 to T6) and 11 adds two plus one more cycle after the strobe (T1 to T7).

operation.topic: ALE in the last access cycle
operation.text: ALE pulses in the cycle after an access (T4 to T7) only when the next instruction reaches RAM, internal or external.

The typical curves are not tested in production. Current was measured with every I/O pin an input with its internal pull-up on, clocked by a rail-to-rail sine wave generator. In active and idle measurements every PRR bit is set, turning the I/O modules off, and the analog comparator is off. Power-down current does not depend on the clock source. Current grows with supply voltage, frequency, pin loading and switching, the code run and temperature, with voltage and frequency the largest factors. Parts are characterised above their tested frequency but only guaranteed to the frequency of their ordering code. The watchdog's own current is the difference between power-down with and without the watchdog timer.

Each module turned on through the power reduction register adds current in active and idle mode. The added current is given as typical absolute figures at three supply and clock points and as a share of active or idle current with an external clock; the absolute figures let the added current be worked out for other supplies and frequencies.

operation.topic: Erratum: differential ADC at 200× gain (ATmega640 rev. A and B, ATmega1280 rev. A, ATmega1281 rev. A)
operation.text: With AVCC below 3.6 V some conversions at random come out wrong, the typical absolute accuracy reaching 64 LSB. There is no workaround.

operation.topic: Erratum: high sleep current (ATmega640 rev. A and B, ATmega1280 rev. A and B, ATmega1281 rev. A and B, ATmega2560 rev. C, ATmega2561 rev. C)
operation.text: Running SLEEP straight after SEI raises the sleep current when an interrupt is pending that cannot wake the part from the chosen sleep mode. Workaround: disable the interrupts that are not wake-up sources before going to sleep.

operation.topic: Erratum: 200× differential gain not working (ATmega2560 rev. F, ATmega2561 rev. F)
operation.text: The 46 dB (200×) amplification of the ADC differential input does not work. There is no workaround.

operation.topic: Erratum: No-Read-While-Write flash (ATmega2560 rev. A, ATmega2561 rev. A)
operation.text: Reading the No-Read-While-Write area of flash is too slow for the part's speed, so that area does not work as intended. Workaround: use only the first 248K of flash; where boot code is needed, run the code in that area at no more than a quarter of the highest frequency for the supply, set through CLKPR before entering the boot section.

operation.topic: Erratum: no operation below 2.4 V (ATmega2560 rev. A, ATmega2561 rev. A)
operation.text: Code does not execute correctly with the supply under 2.4 V. Workaround: keep the supply at 2.4 V or above.

operation.topic: Erratum: differential ADC noise (ATmega2560 rev. A, ATmega2561 rev. A)
operation.text: In differential mode the ADC is noisy, with errors up to 7 LSB. Workaround: keep only the 7 most significant bits of each differential result.

operation.topic: Erratum: internal ADC reference low (ATmega2560 rev. A, ATmega2561 rev. A)
operation.text: The internal ADC reference comes out below its specified value. Workaround: use AVCC or an external reference, or convert a known voltage against the internal reference and use the result to calibrate later conversions.

operation.topic: Erratum: IN/OUT run twice with the stack in external RAM (ATmega2560 rev. A, ATmega2561 rev. A)
operation.text: When the stack pointer lies in external RAM, an IN or OUT executed just before an interrupt runs twice. Effects include SREG reading with I clear, a write to a PIN register toggling the port twice, and interrupt flags reading as cleared. Workaround, either one: use LD/LDS/LDD and ST/STS/STD in place of IN and OUT, or keep the stack in internal RAM.

operation.topic: Erratum: EEPROM read in lock bit mode 3 (ATmega2560 rev. A, ATmega2561 rev. A)
operation.text: With lock bits LB2 and LB1 programmed to mode 3, application code cannot read the EEPROM. Workaround: do not use protection mode 3 where the application reads EEPROM.
